summary:
AstroChronoscope is a public web tool for exploring NASA's SPHEREx sky images over time. A user enters coordinates or picks a known target, and the app searches NASA/IPAC IRSA for real SPHEREx observations of that patch of sky. It groups the results into observation epochs, shows which of the six infrared bands are available, and builds a timeline from the first pass to the last. 

The user can open a FITS cutout, inspect the science image and its flag, variance and PSF extensions, then compare two epochs on the same sky grid. Before subtracting, the app checks WCS alignment, coverage, units and PSF compatibility, and produces a difference image with uncertainty and mask files. 

Everything comes from the live archive, with no mock data. The tool makes a very large survey usable without a research pipeline, so anyone can see how a star, brown dwarf, asteroid or other object has moved or changed brightness between visits. It also keeps the quality checks visible so the results can be trusted.
details:
AstroChronoscope

AstroChronoscope is a web-based astronomical investigation platform that allows users to explore the same region of the sky across multiple SPHEREx observations. Users can enter celestial coordinates (right ascension and declination), define a search radius, or select from predefined astronomical benchmark targets, including Barnard's Star, Epsilon Indi B, WISE 0855−0714, RW Aurigae, and R Draconis.

The browser communicates with a FastAPI backend, which queries the NASA/IPAC Infrared Science Archive (IRSA) through its Simple Image Access (SIA2) service to retrieve genuine SPHEREx observations. The backend parses the returned VOTable metadata, removes duplicate products, groups observations sharing an observation ID into epochs, and orders them chronologically.

The Discovery workspace presents these observations as an interactive timeline, including available SPHEREx spectral bands, exposure information, calibration levels, observation dates, and target-footprint coverage. This allows users to identify suitable observation epochs before downloading and processing the underlying data.

Figure 1. SPHEREx observation discovery showing the R Draconis benchmark target, observation inventory, available spectral bands, observation epochs, and target-footprint coverage.

Selecting an observation retrieves a real FITS cutout through the IRSA Image Server (IBE) cutout service. The backend validates its celestial World Coordinate System (WCS), checks whether the requested target falls within the image footprint, and generates a preview for the browser. Users can also inspect the underlying FITS structure, including science images, quality flags, variance maps, effective PSF information, image statistics, and relevant headers.

Figure 2. FITS Image Explorer displaying a real SPHEREx cutout, pixel-flux statistics, WCS astrometry, and available FITS extensions.

Differential Image Analysis

The central feature of AstroChronoscope is its multi-epoch differential image analysis workflow.

Users select two observations, designated Epoch A and Epoch B. The backend retrieves their FITS cutouts, validates their scientific metadata, checks image coverage and units, evaluates PSF compatibility, and reprojects Epoch B onto the reference pixel grid of Epoch A.

It then measures image alignment using phase correlation, estimates background levels, and evaluates optional photometric scaling where supported. The pipeline generates a difference image:

D = I_B − α × I_A

It also produces associated uncertainty and mask FITS products.

Figure 3. Pairwise epoch comparison showing the reference image, target image, and generated difference product.

Every comparison includes explicit scientific quality checks reported as PASS, WARNING, FAIL, or NOT_VERIFIED. The resulting images, metadata, quality assessments, and provenance information are available for inspection and download.

This workflow provides an accessible way to investigate possible changes between observations, including moving objects, variable sources, and transient candidates, without requiring users to write their own image-processing code.

Scientific limitations are made visible rather than hidden. Alignment residuals are measured rather than automatically corrected, PSF matching uses a global approximation, and image reprojection does not model all sources of correlated uncertainty. A successful computation is therefore not automatically a scientifically validated detection.

Time-Domain and Spectral Analysis

AstroChronoscope extends beyond differential imaging through additional analysis capabilities exposed by the same backend API.

  • Source Detection: Identifies compact sources in SPHEREx images using background estimation, matched filtering, thresholding, segmentation, and basic deblending.
  • Aperture Photometry: Measures source fluxes using circular apertures, local background estimation, and available variance information.
  • Light Curves: Associates sources across observations and constructs per-band time series, including non-detection information.
  • Variability Analysis: Calculates statistical indicators such as fractional variability, chi-square, and median absolute deviation to help identify potentially variable sources.
  • Spectral Analysis: Extracts spectra from SPHEREx DR1 all-sky spectral cubes and supports wavelength-grid-based spectral comparison.
  • Gaia DR3 Integration: Queries Gaia astrometric and photometric data, performs coordinate cross-matching, and supports proper-motion propagation.

These capabilities make the platform useful beyond an initial image comparison. Users can move from observation discovery to source measurements, temporal analysis, spectral inspection, and external catalogue cross-matching.

Figure 4. Time-domain analysis showing associated sources, multi-epoch photometric measurements, light curves, and variability telemetry.

Figure 5. SPHEREx DR1 spectral analysis displaying the extracted 102-channel spectrum across six infrared bands, with individual channel measurements.

An important scientific distinction is that the SPHEREx DR1 all-sky spectral cube is a static mosaic. Comparing extracted spectra does not, by itself, establish temporal spectral variability. Similarly, variability metrics and source associations are investigative evidence, not automatic astrophysical classifications.

Benchmark Target Investigation

AstroChronoscope includes predefined benchmark target configurations to make astronomical investigation easier to start.

The available targets are:

  • Barnard's Star
  • Epsilon Indi B
  • WISE 0855−0714
  • RW Aurigae
  • R Draconis

Each preset provides reference coordinates, search-radius settings, object information, aliases, and catalogue references. Proper-motion information is also available where applicable, with an option to propagate coordinates to the configured mission epoch.

These presets provide convenient starting points for exploring known astronomical objects and testing the platform's observation-discovery and analysis workflows. They do not represent confirmed detections by AstroChronoscope.

Synchronous Operation Monitor

The platform includes a centralized Operation Monitor that tracks backend API operations across the application.

It records operation names, categories, workspaces, target or source context, start times, execution durations, completion states, and failure diagnostics.

Because the scientific backend currently uses synchronous request-response operations, the monitor reports actual request lifecycle states rather than presenting fabricated percentage-based progress. This gives users visibility into active and completed scientific processing requests while navigating between workspaces.

Motivation and Intended Impact

SPHEREx repeatedly surveys the entire sky, producing valuable infrared observations across multiple spectral bands. However, accessing archive products, understanding FITS files, and performing multi-epoch image analysis can be challenging for students, citizen scientists, and researchers who do not regularly work with astronomical data-processing software.

AstroChronoscope turns these steps into a guided, visual investigation workflow. It connects real archive observations to image inspection, differential analysis, source measurements, light curves, spectral exploration, and catalogue cross-matching while keeping scientific quality checks and data provenance visible.

The project is particularly relevant to investigating moving or changing astronomical sources, including potential distant Solar System objects associated with the Planet X challenge.

AstroChronoscope does not claim to discover or confirm Planet Nine, asteroids, or transient events. Instead, it provides an accessible and reproducible way to identify interesting observational evidence that can be examined through further scientific analysis.

The frontend runs as a browser-based application, while computationally intensive astronomical processing is handled by the Python backend. Users do not need a local astronomical data-processing environment or specialized hardware to use the platform.

Technology Stack and Resources

Frontend: React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS 4, and Three.js for the interactive landing-page visualization.

Backend: Python 3.14+, FastAPI, Pydantic, Astropy, NumPy, SciPy, Matplotlib, Pillow, Requests, and urllib3.

Astronomical data and services:

  • NASA/IPAC IRSA SIA2 for SPHEREx observation discovery.
  • NASA/IPAC IRSA Image Server (IBE) for FITS product retrieval and spatial cutouts.
  • SPHEREx Quick Release 3 (QR3) observations for multi-epoch image analysis.
  • SPHEREx Data Release 1 (DR1) all-sky spectral cubes for spectral extraction.
  • ESA Gaia Data Release 3 (DR3), accessed through its Table Access Protocol (TAP), for astrometric and photometric catalogue queries.

Testing: The backend includes a deterministic automated test suite and separate opt-in live integration tests against external astronomical archives. This separates reproducible software validation from tests that depend on external network services.

What Makes the Project Creative

AstroChronoscope presents astronomical investigation through a mission-control-inspired interface. Its features include a live UTC and Modified Julian Date (MJD) clock, interactive observation timelines, spectral-band filters, celestial targeting controls, benchmark target presets, image inspection, and side-by-side epoch comparison.

A targeting reticle provides spatial context over image cutouts, while the differential analysis workflow turns two archive observations into a downloadable difference image and associated scientific products.

The centralized Operation Monitor provides visibility into backend processing without pretending that synchronous requests have intermediate progress information.

The interface is designed to make the scientific process understandable rather than simply displaying visually appealing astronomical imagery. Quality checks, warnings, provenance, and processing limitations are treated as core parts of the experience.

Factors Considered During Development

The project was developed with emphasis on:

  • Data authenticity: Using genuine SPHEREx observations and external catalogue data rather than fabricated observations.
  • Scientific correctness: Validating celestial WCS, image units, target coverage, masks, variance information, and comparison prerequisites.
  • Transparent quality assessment: Reporting warnings, failures, and unverified conditions instead of silently presenting every result as scientifically valid.
  • Reproducibility: Recording input provenance, checksums, processing parameters, and software-version information for derived products.
  • Performance and reliability: Applying download limits, timeouts, retries, caching, and bounded processing workloads.
  • External service resilience: Handling archive outages, temporary HTTP failures, malformed responses, and unavailable observations.
  • Modular architecture: Keeping the frontend independent of the scientific backend through a documented REST API, allowing the processing pipeline to be tested and reused independently.

AstroChronoscope aims to make real astronomical archive data easier to investigate while preserving the scientific context needed to interpret the results responsibly.
